DNA Database

By: Sasha OLD | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What if you were forced to give your DNA to ensure that South Africa can rid itself of crime?

Unique Selling Point:
Well this may be South Africa's future and what Police Minister Bheki Cele wants. So what's the problem? They current CRIMINAL DNA database hasn't even completed the testing of Schedule 8 offenders and Cele has suspended that program while he waits to politicize the issue.
1. A backlog of 46,727 Schedule 8 offenders (highest level of danger) who were in jail before the DNA Act (2013) took effect, and therefore have been there for a minimum of 6 years, which shows these were serious crimes because a 6-year or longer sentence is fairly hefty in the SA context. It is not about all offenders - they are being tested when they are arrested or sentenced. It is about the backlog of Schedule 8s who are being paroled or released without being tested.
2. the constitutionality of Cele’s proposed national population DNA database (as opposed to a forensic one, which we have). No country in the world has managed to force every single innocent citizen to submit to DNA testing as it has been ruled unconstitutional. In SA, many experts say it would contravene the Bill of Rights;
3. Why Bheki Cele will not authorise the testing of the convicts while simultaneously exploring the total population DNA database idea;
4. It is about where the money - absolute minimum R5 billion - would come from, AND where is the R20 million that was meant to cover the convict backlog testing? I don’t know the answers re the money.

IN the current climate of a veritable war on women and children, and with 58 murders and 114 reported rapes every day, unleashing a violent demographic upon the public without even taking their DNA fingerprint seems irresponsible at best, yet that is precisely what is happening. And the one man - police minister Bheki Cele - who can rectify this has declined to do so.




Summary:
Tens of thousands of dangerous convicts are being released from prison each year but not all of their DNA profiles have been recorded. These profiles would enable law enforcement to potentially match their DNA to other crimes they may have committed, cold cases, as well as any crimes committed by the same offender in future.

The Department of Correctional Services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled last year. In addition, many schedule eight offenders — those convicted of murder, culpable homicide, rape, kidnapping, sexual offences against children, human trafficking, assault, robbery and arson — were released without the department collecting their DNA profiles.

Cele has failed to sign the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Amendment Bill, drawn up last year, which would allow correctional services officials to take samples of a backlog of 46,727 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA who remain untested. Instead, Cele has declined to sign the amendment bill in favour of moving towards an unprecedented national population DNA database that would require every South African citizen to have a DNA test by way of a buccal (saliva) test. This would then be the mandate of the Department of Home Affairs.
Cele's refusal to sign the amendment bill indicates a change of heart since his foreward in the DNA Ethics and Oversight Board's annual report in September last year, in which he wrote that "focus will also be placed on finalising the amendment to the DNA Act which aims to address shortcomings related to the retrospective sampling of offenders serving a sentence for [serious crimes]”.
Cele had at that time agreed that the amendment was needed after a two-year "transitional period" expired.




Further information:
"The continuation of the convicted offender sampling programme is essential as the convicted offender index on the National Forensic DNA Database provides an important link to resolving cold cases and apprehending repeat offenders... The conviction and sentencing of serial rapist Sikhangele Mki in September 2017 to 15 life terms demonstrates the importance of ensuring that all convicted offenders are sampled," Cele wrote.
The transitional period expired in 2017, leaving more than 46,500 schedule eight convicts unprocessed for DNA. The DCS and the police were not able to process the numbers of prisoners in time because of hold-ups caused by computer interfacing glitches between the departments of police and correctional services, exacerbated by a crippling shortage of sampling kits.
Cele's spokesperson Lirandzu Themba said his about-turn was based on advice by the Justice, Crime Prevention & Security. (JCPS) Cluster that “the country embark on a national sampling of all citizens to assist in having a proper DNA database to assist when crime is committed”.

However, the constitutionality of Cele's desire for a national DNA database has been called into question by the DA, whose police spokesperson Andrew Whitfield called for the backlog of convicts to be sampled in the short term.
"While national government drags its feet on this issue, potential repeat offenders are being released back into society, while SAPS remains with no means of tracking whether these individuals are repeating the offences they were originally convicted of," he said in a statement last month.
"The introduction of this bill will add impetus to our fight against gender-based violence. It will ensure that the time needed to convict a repeat offender is minimised, thereby serving justice to victims faster and more efficiently, while freeing up resources for SAPS to pursue more cases and convict more felons.”

Whitfield said a national population DNA database was unaffordable, unconstitutional, violated the Bill of Rights, and “wholly unnecessary for the tabling of this Bill”.

In an e-mail (which this journalist has in their possession) to a number of high-ranking Saps officials on September 18 this year, Major-General Matilda Manamela of Saps’s Forensic Services Division reminded them that: “The State Law Advisor had advised the Portfolio Committee on Police at the time, during the deliberation of the DNA Bill, that it will not be constitutional for the DNA database to include the population at large.”

However, Themba told the Sunday Times that Cele was of the opinion that “only the Constitutional Court can decide on the constitutionality of any matter".
Cele declined to explain why the proposed population database precluded the backlog of criminals from being tested in the meantime.

Vanessa Lynch, founder of The DNA Project who lobbied support for the for the passing of the DNA Act (in 2013) believes that, at the very least, parolees leaving prison should in the meantime be sampled prior to being released.
“If a simple amendment was signed whereby convicted offenders eligible for parole were compelled to submit their sample before being released from prison, this would ensure that serial offenders would be apprehended before committing further crimes, as well as assist with cold cases,” said Lynch.
In the current environment where gender-based violence is rife, she believes this to be a reasonable interim solution whilst a White Paper on a population database could be drafted for review without the risk of vulnerable women and children falling prey to serial offenders who could have been identified though DNA before being released.

DCS spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo said the only figures the department had were that 143,260 convicts were released over the past two years, but he could not provide figures of how many of those were schedule eight offenders or how many had DNA samples taken. The DCS could also not provide any figures on how many were repeat offenders.


Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout of the Department of Social Work and Criminology at the University of Pretoria said while no official government figures for recidivism existed, academic studies put the chances of schedule eight offenders committing further crimes on release or parole at 94%.
"South Africa has one of the highest crime rates in the world, as well as some of the highest numbers of incarcerated people, and a very poor rehabilitation programme. In addition, the average criminal in South Africa commits around 100 crimes before being caught. The risk to reward ratio is astoundingly in favour of criminals being tempted back into a life of crime. Prison is the university of crime where, far from being rehabilitated, they learn the tricks of the trade from others and in fact hone their 'skills'. And, most of all, they learn how to justify their criminal behaviour to themselves," said Bezuidenhout.
Professor Rudolph Zinn of the Department of Police Practice at Unisa, who has interviewed violent offenders in jail for the past 16 years, said his studies have shown that "criminals generally commit several types of crimes: those caught for robbery also turn out to be rapists and murderers".
Bezuidenhout added that, "If a person rapes once, he will do it again".
"There is a serial rapist in every rapist. They are virtually unrehabilitatable, especially after having been to prison. They do not learn from their mistakes or from punishment. In addition, violence is so systemic in our jails that they are themselves victimised and traumatised while incarcerated, damaging them further," he said.
Cape Town mayoral council member for safety and security, JP Smith, expressed concern about the number of "gangsters" being released from jail in the province.
"It used to be about 75 offenders being released every week. Now it is more than 450," he said.
Smith cited the recent murder of Russian visitor Ivan Ivanov, who was stabbed to death on Chapman's Peak in July, 10 metres from a parking lot at the start of a hiking trail. One of the three men arrested for the murder had been paroled less than 48 hours earlier for a prior murder conviction.
"We are creating our own gang war here," said Smith.

[The matter was brought to the attention of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s but spokesperson Khusela Diko said he had declined to comment on any of these issues, and merely referred the questions back to Cele.]


SIDEBAR

Police Minister Bheki Cele's spokesperson Lirandzhu Themba said Cele had written to the Home Affairs ministry seven months ago "about the feasibility of taking samples for the whole population and not only from convicted offenders".
"This would be the competency of Home Affairs and not that of the police department. The police ministry is still waiting for a response on this matter," she said.

But it transpired that the correspondence from Cele had not been seen until the DHA was asked for comment. Home Affairs Minister Aaron Motsoaledi said, “The letter from Minister Bheki Cele to the Department of Home Affairs, on February 7 2019 was addressed to the then minister of Home Affairs, Dr Siyabonga Cwele.

As Minister of Home Affairs since May 28 2019, I was not aware of this letter, but it was given to me after this query by this journalist. We (minister of Home Affairs, minister of Health, and the Health Ombudsman) did not see the letter addressed to former Home Affairs minister Cwele, but now we are all of common mind with Minister Cele about the development of a population DNA database. We will all work together to make this a possibility.

“I must state that I am very much in favour of a population DNA database. Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize has also discussed the possibility of a population DNA database because he is also interested in it. Separately, Health Ombudsman Professor Malegapuru Makgoba also phoned me to ask about the possibility of such a venture. He told me that he is investigating internationally what the practice is.

“I met with the Minister of Health and our respective teams on August 5 2019 to discuss a programme whereby new-borns will not be allowed to leave hospitals after birth without an unabridged birth certificate. The possibility of collecting DNA samples at the same time was also discussed.

>>> In terms of finance, one buccal swab in the form of an EasiCollect device with an FTA card costs a minimum of R85, says Dr Laura Heathfield, a forensic genetics expert at UCT. Thus, by extrapolation, a minimum of R5 billion will be required to test all 58 million people in the country. This is only the cost of the sample collection device and not laboratory analysis, and also does not take into consideration the substantial infrastructure that would be required for testing, such as centres and laboratories, and the employment of staff to do the tests.




MY COMMENTS AND SOME EXPLANATORY NOTES

I can also tell you what the international practice is which Makgoba says he is looking into: It has been proposed in many countries, especially first-world ones, but so far the suggestion that every single innocent person be forced to give their genetic information to the state has been declared unconstitutional and an infringement on the right to privacy… eg. Portugal, UAE, France, Canada.

1. No country has yet managed an entire pop database, only very extensive forensic ones. It would be miraculous if SA was the first country in the world to get a national population database! And some very first-world countries only have 5 million people and they have not managed it, in theory, in law, or in practice.

“In the expansive group [of countries that have a forensic database], the inclusion criteria in most countries allow that individuals suspected of any crime can be submitted to sample collection and, consequently, to the inclusion of their respective DNA profiles in the forensic database.”

and

“[Internationally] the ethical challenges of forensic DNA databases have usually been approached as potential threats to a range of civil rights, such as the right to privacy, liberty and moral and physical integrity, the dignity of persons, and the presumption of innocence.”

https://jme.bmj.com/content/41/10/820.info
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6533668/



2. We have already seen in SA that police officers could not be tested (to exclude their DNA from crime scenes) as it was seen to be an infringement of their rights.

3. Even in forensic (ie criminal databases) there are strict codes that apply to discarding genetic info if a person is found innocent, or after a certain period of time after they have been released, etc. So criminals’ rights to genetic privacy are considered worldwide — how then would innocent citizens feel about being forced to provide their genetic data?

4. [Getting into what can be done with people’s private genetic info is obviously way beyond the scope of this article, but if not strictly regulated, it can be sold to medical companies, planted at crime scenes, as well as used to discriminate on grounds of race or gender, among other concerns.]

Here is a mail from Brigadier Marga van Rooyen, SAPS Division of Legal and Policy Services, an expert academic and author in law of evidence, who clearly does NOT recommend a total population DNA database for a variety of reasons:

Good Day Aly

Kindly find the below response

1. Privacy concerns. The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPI Act) was passed in Parliament and is awaiting the proclamation of the President to come into operation. This Act aims to protect personal information of persons and places stringent obligations on the state to ensure the safekeeping, storage and destruction of personal information. A database of DNA will be subjected to the stringent requirements and obligations as set out in the POPI Act. This includes considerations such as the purpose for which the DNA database will kept and what the purpose of the database will be, for what purpose it may it be utilised, the time period for which the personal information may be kept etc. All these requirements will have to be considered to determine the legal implications and feasibility of such a database;

2. During the deliberations of the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Bill in Parliament in 2013, a proposal was made that the DNA of all police officials should be taken. This proposal was rejected in the Portfolio Committee based on considerations of privacy and the financial implications of the proposal. A national database will increase these considerations substantially.

3. Another concern raised in Parliament at that time, was the risk that the police may "plant" the DNA of an innocent person on a crime scene to implicate him in an offence. A national database will increase this risk or the potential that the police will be able to do so. It order to ensure the integrity of the database, proper measures will have to be included to ensure limited access to the database and to protect the safekeeping and storage of the DNA to prevent interference or manipulation thereof. It will pose serious risks to the investigation of offences if DNA may be removed or stolen and there is a perception that the DNA of an innocent person may have been planted at a crime scene; and

4. Legal processes will have to be included to ensure that every person submits a DNA sample. The enforceability of such a requirement will have serious legal implications. Clarification will have to obtained on measures which will be implemented in a person, for example, refuses to submit a sample voluntarily. The legal implication of any enforcement measure will have to comply with constitutional considerations. It is, for example, doubtful that the law will permit a person to be forced to submit a DNA sample against his will. Another consideration in this regard will be the taking and storage of the DNA of undocumented persons and how these matters will be enforced.

In view of the above, it is clear that the proposal has serious legal implications.

With respect
Marga van Rooyen

Script:


DNA is a unique identifier that is used as a forensic tool to match a known suspects blood or semen to a sample taken from a crime scene or a rape victim.
Vanessa: “The DNA project was an organization I founded in 2004 following the murder of my father.”
Vanessa Lynch says police never solved her fathers murder, after he was killed during a home invasion. As police never collected forensic evidence, up until now no one has been convicted.
Vanessa: “The reason why I started the DNA project was that I understood that in my father's death that nothing I would do would bring him back personally but I did understand that there were so many people in South Africa that had been affected by crime much the same as our family was affected by crime. And I put a lot of energy and passion into trying to alleviate that situation.”
This need to make a chance, resulted in her lobbying government create a criminal DNA database.
Vanessa: “Forensic DNA profiling was such a useful forensic tool to resolve murders to solve cold cases. We didn't have the awareness in South Africa to really utilize this incredible technology.”
THESE PROFILES WOULD ENABLE LAW ENFORCEMENT TO POTENTIALLY MATCH THEIR DNA TO OTHER CRIMES THEY MAY HAVE COMMITTED, COLD CASES, AS WELL AS OTHER CRIMES THEY MAY COMMIT IN THE FUTURE.
University of Pretoria criminologist Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout who has studied violent offenders for 27 years, says they commit many crimes before they’re caught.
Bezuidenhout: “On average 100-105 crimes are committed before they're apprehended. Bezuidenhout: “So they’ll start over with the smaller crime, snatch and grab like a mobile phone, and they escalate. We think that many rapists are actually serial rapist, because they get away with it.”
That is why convicted offenders were a priority during the discussions resulting in the DNA bill.
Vanessa: “The original portfolio committee when passing the bill wanted the convicted offender population to be on the database because they understood that it was a very important part of the forensic DNA database. Recently there was a case for instance of McKee. He was arrested and convicted of an assault for a period of eleven months. His sample was taken at the time that it was able to be taken and that profile was entered onto the convicted offender database. It linked him to 30 unsolved rapes.”
The database was a great success - connecting perpetrators to both current and past crimes, but then the testing abruptly ended.
Vanessa: “Unfortunately due to issues such as systems not interfacing and training issues they weren't able to put that population on the database within two years.”
To fix this, in 2018, the criminal law amendment bill was created allowing correctional services officials to sample the backlog of nearly 47,000 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA - that remain untested.
IN THE CURRENT CLIMATE OF A WAR ON WOMEN AND CHILDREN, AND WITH 58 MURDERS AND 114 REPORTED RAPES EVERY DAY, UNLEASHING A VIOLENT DEMOGRAPHIC UPON THE PUBLIC WITHOUT EVEN TAKING THEIR DNA AND FINGERPRINTS SEEMS IRRESPONSIBLE AT BEST, YET THAT IS PRECISELY WHAT IS HAPPENING. AND THE ONE MAN - POLICE MINISTER BHEKI CELE - WHO CAN RECTIFY THIS, HAS DECLINED TO DO SO.
Vanessa: “It was simply a technical amendment that was requested of the minister, to say extend this so that we can continue to sample convicted offenders.”
THEY WERE INMATES WHO WERE IN JAIL BEFORE THE DNA ACT OF 2013 TOOK EFFECT, AND THEREFORE HAVE BEEN THERE FOR A MINIMUM OF 6 YEARS.
Journalist Aly Verbaan has reported on the DNA bill extensively, she says initially Minister Cele agreed the amendment was needed.
Verbaan: “On the board's annual report he wrote a about how important it is that he signs this and then within four months, completely turned around.”
INSTEAD, CELE HAS DECLINED TO SIGN THE AMENDMENT BILL IN FAVOUR OF MOVING TOWARDS AN UNPRECEDENTED NATIONAL POPULATION DNA DATABASE THAT WOULD REQUIRE EVERY SOUTH AFRICAN CITIZEN TO HAVE A DNA TEST BY WAY OF A BUCCAL SWAB TEST. THIS WOULD THEN BE THE MANDATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HOME AFFAIRS.
In February 2019 General Bheki Cele wrote to the Department of Home Affairs after the idea of a population database - containing everyone’s DNA - was proposed during a cabinet committee meeting. Cele’s reasoning for the database was to address the “urgent need to strengthen the country’s crime fighting capacity and conviction of criminals.”
Vanessa: “A population database as is a is a fairly controversial idea. It hasn't been enabled anywhere in the world simply because the idea of including all citizens DNA on a database is, it's not something that would would pass constitutional muster.”
This is because it would arguably contravene the basic human right to privacy, because our genetic information may be sold or used unethically says Forensic Geneticist Dr Laura Heathfield.
Heathfield: “Our legislation has addressed many of the ethical issues surrounding a DNA database for example it stipulates that the DNA sample which contains the full genetic makeup of an individual must be destroyed after a certain period of time.”
Vanessa: The difficulty with this approach whilst in theory it probably sounds like a really good idea. Is that you are now undermining the very nature of the retention framework that currently exists in South Africa, because the portfolio committee who were passing the DNA bill originally did not want innocent persons profiles to remain on the database.”
Even the police’s own legal department questioned its constitutionality.
IN AN EMAIL TO A NUMBER OF HIGH-RANKING SAPS OFFICIALS IN SEPTEMBER THIS YEAR, THEY WERE REMINDED THAT DURING THE DELIBERATION OF THE DNA BILL, THE STATE LAW ADVISOR HAD ADVISED THE PORTFOLIO COMMITTEE ON POLICE, THAT “IT WILL NOT BE CONSTITUTIONAL FOR THE DNA DATABASE TO INCLUDE THE ENTIRE POPULATION.”
Verbaan: “It's a non sequitur to say that we are not testing the people who are already guilty of Schedule 8 crimes, and what we're going to do instead is focus on the whole country; we're going to test newborn babies in hospitals, 58 million people, the vast majority of whom have done nothing wrong. How on earth are you going to get people on the street to voluntarily go and give their DNA, their genetic information, to a government?”
The department of correctional services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled in 2018.
IN ADDITION, MANY SCHEDULE EIGHT OFFENDERS — THOSE CONVICTED OF MURDER, CULPABLE HOMICIDE, RAPE, KIDNAPPING, SEXUAL OFFENCES AGAINST CHILDREN, HUMAN TRAFFICKING, ASSAULT, ROBBERY AND ARSON — WERE RELEASED WITHOUT THEIR DNA PROFILES BEING COLLECTED.
Verbaan: “You can collect the DNA at the crime scene but you've got nothing to match it to. We already have them in jail and there’s a law which requires them to give us their DNA. It's just absolutely inexplicable that we can't just get that done.”
Studies show that violent criminals are roughly 85-95 percent more likely to reoffend.
Bezuidenhout: “If you have a person in prison. 10 years they'll go through all the rehabilitation programs they get out two weeks later they commit the same crime. Jeffrey Thompson, the recent case that killed the elderly couple in Cape Town, he was out on parole and two days later you know commit the crime.
Thompson was subsequently sentenced to two life terms, plus 58 years for these murders. The high reoffending rate can be attributed to the lack of prisoner rehabilitation.
Bezuidenhout: “We have a very high prison rate, we can accommodate 130,000, we in 165,000. You must have enough professionals; social workers psychologists - the ratio must be very low so that you've got proper professional intervention.”
The collection of DNA is a relatively simple process.
Heathfield: “We use what's called an easy collect device, and we collect DNA using this foam applicator on the inside of the individual's cheek.”
Heathfield calculated the potential cost of just testing the DNA for a national population database.
Heathfield: “An Easy collect device costs R163.25. So to just take a sample from a population of 58 million people would cost approximately nine and a half billion rand. And then for DNA profile it would usually cost between 750 and 1000 rand. And it's best practice to do the test in duplicate. So if we're conservative, we would look at an additional 87 billion rand. So altogether over 96 billion rand as a baseline.”
FIGURES SHOW THAT 143,260 CONVICTS WERE RELEASED OVER THE PAST TWO YEARS, BUT HOW MANY OF THOSE WERE SCHEDULE EIGHT OFFENDERS OR HOW MANY HAD DNA SAMPLES TAKEN IS UNKNOWN. THE DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONAL SERVICES COULD ALSO NOT PROVIDE ANY FIGURES ON HOW MANY WERE REPEAT OFFENDERS.
Aly: “There are people getting out today whose DNA we have not taken who are literally going to kill somebody this week. And that's not that's not my opinion. It's a fact. And this is going to take years even if we got this through the constitution. So here we're going to have schedule eight criminals knowing that they are not on the record.”
MINISTER CELE DECLINED AN INTERVIEW WITH CARTE BLANCHE, BECAUSE HE BELIEVES THE DECISION TO HAVE A POPULATION DATABASE LIES WITH THE CONSTITUTIONAL COURT. CELE DID NOT EXPLAIN WHY THE PROPOSED POPULATION DATABASE PRECLUDED THE BACKLOG OF CRIMINALS FROM BEING TESTED IN THE MEANTIME.
Aly: “That's the simple question. So the answer keeps coming back. No we were handing it over to Home Affairs.”
Like Verbaan we were also referred to the department of home affairs. It says the concept is under consideration and there’s no clear answer yet. The department told Verbaan they had not received Minister Cele’s February letter that proposed the population database. She sent it again, and was surprised by the departmental spokespersons’ quick response.
Verbaan: “They dug it, he read the mail on thursday, on the friday,.within a day he'd made up his mind that they're yes they're going to do this, and they seemed to think they’re gonna add DNA database with 58 million people, onto the fingerprints system.”
However, Bezuidenhout thinks a population database may be the only way to curb our high crime rate.
Bezuidenhout: “My opinion and it might be controversial. I think a database needs to work like fingerprints. Everybody needs to donate DNA. It’s those individuals that raped, a serial, once or two or three, it’s those individuals that got away with stuff that must be worried.”
Vanessa: “The immediate solution definitely would be to enable a technical amendment to allow the police to sample parolees prior to them being released from prison. And that if the ministry was very serious about a population database that can happen in parallel to it. When the DNA Act passed I felt it was a victory for a number of South Africans because here was a methodology that could really really identify serial offenders and stop them from continuing to perpetuate crime against vulnerable vulnerable citizens of South Africa. It upsets me terribly that we are not giving it the resources and the dedication that it that it should have in order for us to really do something about crime.

Unique Selling Point: Well this may be South Africa's future and what Police Minister Bheki Cele wants. So what's the problem? They current CRIMINAL DNA database hasn't even completed the testing of Schedule 8 offenders and Cele has suspended that program while he waits to politicize the issue. 1. A backlog of 46,727 Schedule 8 offenders (highest level of danger) who were in jail before the DNA Act (2013) took effect, and therefore have been there for a minimum of 6 years, which shows these were serious crimes because a 6-year or longer sentence is fairly hefty in the SA context. It is not about all offenders - they are being tested when they are arrested or sentenced. It is about the backlog of Schedule 8s who are being paroled or released without being tested. 2. the constitutionality of Cele’s proposed national population DNA database (as opposed to a forensic one, which we have). No country in the world has managed to force every single innocent citizen to submit to DNA testing as it has been ruled unconstitutional. In SA, many experts say it would contravene the Bill of Rights; 3. Why Bheki Cele will not authorise the testing of the convicts while simultaneously exploring the total population DNA database idea; 4. It is about where the money - absolute minimum R5 billion - would come from, AND where is the R20 million that was meant to cover the convict backlog testing? I don’t know the answers re the money. IN the current climate of a veritable war on women and children, and with 58 murders and 114 reported rapes every day, unleashing a violent demographic upon the public without even taking their DNA fingerprint seems irresponsible at best, yet that is precisely what is happening. And the one man - police minister Bheki Cele - who can rectify this has declined to do so. Summary: Tens of thousands of dangerous convicts are being released from prison each year but not all of their DNA profiles have been recorded. These profiles would enable law enforcement to potentially match their DNA to other crimes they may have committed, cold cases, as well as any crimes committed by the same offender in future. The Department of Correctional Services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled last year. In addition, many schedule eight offenders — those convicted of murder, culpable homicide, rape, kidnapping, sexual offences against children, human trafficking, assault, robbery and arson — were released without the department collecting their DNA profiles. Cele has failed to sign the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Amendment Bill, drawn up last year, which would allow correctional services officials to take samples of a backlog of 46,727 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA who remain untested. Instead, Cele has declined to sign the amendment bill in favour of moving towards an unprecedented national population DNA database that would require every South African citizen to have a DNA test by way of a buccal (saliva) test. This would then be the mandate of the Department of Home Affairs. Cele's refusal to sign the amendment bill indicates a change of heart since his foreward in the DNA Ethics and Oversight Board's annual report in September last year, in which he wrote that "focus will also be placed on finalising the amendment to the DNA Act which aims to address shortcomings related to the retrospective sampling of offenders serving a sentence for [serious crimes]”. Cele had at that time agreed that the amendment was needed after a two-year "transitional period" expired. Further information: "The continuation of the convicted offender sampling programme is essential as the convicted offender index on the National Forensic DNA Database provides an important link to resolving cold cases and apprehending repeat offenders... The conviction and sentencing of serial rapist Sikhangele Mki in September 2017 to 15 life terms demonstrates the importance of ensuring that all convicted offenders are sampled," Cele wrote. The transitional period expired in 2017, leaving more than 46,500 schedule eight convicts unprocessed for DNA. The DCS and the police were not able to process the numbers of prisoners in time because of hold-ups caused by computer interfacing glitches between the departments of police and correctional services, exacerbated by a crippling shortage of sampling kits. Cele's spokesperson Lirandzu Themba said his about-turn was based on advice by the Justice, Crime Prevention & Security. (JCPS) Cluster that “the country embark on a national sampling of all citizens to assist in having a proper DNA database to assist when crime is committed”. However, the constitutionality of Cele's desire for a national DNA database has been called into question by the DA, whose police spokesperson Andrew Whitfield called for the backlog of convicts to be sampled in the short term. "While national government drags its feet on this issue, potential repeat offenders are being released back into society, while SAPS remains with no means of tracking whether these individuals are repeating the offences they were originally convicted of," he said in a statement last month. "The introduction of this bill will add impetus to our fight against gender-based violence. It will ensure that the time needed to convict a repeat offender is minimised, thereby serving justice to victims faster and more efficiently, while freeing up resources for SAPS to pursue more cases and convict more felons.” Whitfield said a national population DNA database was unaffordable, unconstitutional, violated the Bill of Rights, and “wholly unnecessary for the tabling of this Bill”. In an e-mail (which this journalist has in their possession) to a number of high-ranking Saps officials on September 18 this year, Major-General Matilda Manamela of Saps’s Forensic Services Division reminded them that: “The State Law Advisor had advised the Portfolio Committee on Police at the time, during the deliberation of the DNA Bill, that it will not be constitutional for the DNA database to include the population at large.” However, Themba told the Sunday Times that Cele was of the opinion that “only the Constitutional Court can decide on the constitutionality of any matter". Cele declined to explain why the proposed population database precluded the backlog of criminals from being tested in the meantime. Vanessa Lynch, founder of The DNA Project who lobbied support for the for the passing of the DNA Act (in 2013) believes that, at the very least, parolees leaving prison should in the meantime be sampled prior to being released. “If a simple amendment was signed whereby convicted offenders eligible for parole were compelled to submit their sample before being released from prison, this would ensure that serial offenders would be apprehended before committing further crimes, as well as assist with cold cases,” said Lynch. In the current environment where gender-based violence is rife, she believes this to be a reasonable interim solution whilst a White Paper on a population database could be drafted for review without the risk of vulnerable women and children falling prey to serial offenders who could have been identified though DNA before being released. DCS spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo said the only figures the department had were that 143,260 convicts were released over the past two years, but he could not provide figures of how many of those were schedule eight offenders or how many had DNA samples taken. The DCS could also not provide any figures on how many were repeat offenders. Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout of the Department of Social Work and Criminology at the University of Pretoria said while no official government figures for recidivism existed, academic studies put the chances of schedule eight offenders committing further crimes on release or parole at 94%. "South Africa has one of the highest crime rates in the world, as well as some of the highest numbers of incarcerated people, and a very poor rehabilitation programme. In addition, the average criminal in South Africa commits around 100 crimes before being caught. The risk to reward ratio is astoundingly in favour of criminals being tempted back into a life of crime. Prison is the university of crime where, far from being rehabilitated, they learn the tricks of the trade from others and in fact hone their 'skills'. And, most of all, they learn how to justify their criminal behaviour to themselves," said Bezuidenhout. Professor Rudolph Zinn of the Department of Police Practice at Unisa, who has interviewed violent offenders in jail for the past 16 years, said his studies have shown that "criminals generally commit several types of crimes: those caught for robbery also turn out to be rapists and murderers". Bezuidenhout added that, "If a person rapes once, he will do it again". "There is a serial rapist in every rapist. They are virtually unrehabilitatable, especially after having been to prison. They do not learn from their mistakes or from punishment. In addition, violence is so systemic in our jails that they are themselves victimised and traumatised while incarcerated, damaging them further," he said. Cape Town mayoral council member for safety and security, JP Smith, expressed concern about the number of "gangsters" being released from jail in the province. "It used to be about 75 offenders being released every week. Now it is more than 450," he said. Smith cited the recent murder of Russian visitor Ivan Ivanov, who was stabbed to death on Chapman's Peak in July, 10 metres from a parking lot at the start of a hiking trail. One of the three men arrested for the murder had been paroled less than 48 hours earlier for a prior murder conviction. "We are creating our own gang war here," said Smith. Extra Budget Items: flight to cape town [The matter was brought to the attention of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s but spokesperson Khusela Diko said he had declined to comment on any of these issues, and merely referred the questions back to Cele.] SIDEBAR Police Minister Bheki Cele's spokesperson Lirandzhu Themba said Cele had written to the Home Affairs ministry seven months ago "about the feasibility of taking samples for the whole population and not only from convicted offenders". "This would be the competency of Home Affairs and not that of the police department. The police ministry is still waiting for a response on this matter," she said. But it transpired that the correspondence from Cele had not been seen until the DHA was asked for comment. Home Affairs Minister Aaron Motsoaledi said, “The letter from Minister Bheki Cele to the Department of Home Affairs, on February 7 2019 was addressed to the then minister of Home Affairs, Dr Siyabonga Cwele. As Minister of Home Affairs since May 28 2019, I was not aware of this letter, but it was given to me after this query by this journalist. We (minister of Home Affairs, minister of Health, and the Health Ombudsman) did not see the letter addressed to former Home Affairs minister Cwele, but now we are all of common mind with Minister Cele about the development of a population DNA database. We will all work together to make this a possibility. “I must state that I am very much in favour of a population DNA database. Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize has also discussed the possibility of a population DNA database because he is also interested in it. Separately, Health Ombudsman Professor Malegapuru Makgoba also phoned me to ask about the possibility of such a venture. He told me that he is investigating internationally what the practice is. “I met with the Minister of Health and our respective teams on August 5 2019 to discuss a programme whereby new-borns will not be allowed to leave hospitals after birth without an unabridged birth certificate. The possibility of collecting DNA samples at the same time was also discussed. >>> In terms of finance, one buccal swab in the form of an EasiCollect device with an FTA card costs a minimum of R85, says Dr Laura Heathfield, a forensic genetics expert at UCT. Thus, by extrapolation, a minimum of R5 billion will be required to test all 58 million people in the country. This is only the cost of the sample collection device and not laboratory analysis, and also does not take into consideration the substantial infrastructure that would be required for testing, such as centres and laboratories, and the employment of staff to do the tests. MY COMMENTS AND SOME EXPLANATORY NOTES I can also tell you what the international practice is which Makgoba says he is looking into: It has been proposed in many countries, especially first-world ones, but so far the suggestion that every single innocent person be forced to give their genetic information to the state has been declared unconstitutional and an infringement on the right to privacy… eg. Portugal, UAE, France, Canada. 1. No country has yet managed an entire pop database, only very extensive forensic ones. It would be miraculous if SA was the first country in the world to get a national population database! And some very first-world countries only have 5 million people and they have not managed it, in theory, in law, or in practice. “In the expansive group [of countries that have a forensic database], the inclusion criteria in most countries allow that individuals suspected of any crime can be submitted to sample collection and, consequently, to the inclusion of their respective DNA profiles in the forensic database.” and “[Internationally] the ethical challenges of forensic DNA databases have usually been approached as potential threats to a range of civil rights, such as the right to privacy, liberty and moral and physical integrity, the dignity of persons, and the presumption of innocence.” https://jme.bmj.com/content/41/10/820.info https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6533668/ 2. We have already seen in SA that police officers could not be tested (to exclude their DNA from crime scenes) as it was seen to be an infringement of their rights. 3. Even in forensic (ie criminal databases) there are strict codes that apply to discarding genetic info if a person is found innocent, or after a certain period of time after they have been released, etc. So criminals’ rights to genetic privacy are considered worldwide — how then would innocent citizens feel about being forced to provide their genetic data? 4. [Getting into what can be done with people’s private genetic info is obviously way beyond the scope of this article, but if not strictly regulated, it can be sold to medical companies, planted at crime scenes, as well as used to discriminate on grounds of race or gender, among other concerns.] Here is a mail from Brigadier Marga van Rooyen, SAPS Division of Legal and Policy Services, an expert academic and author in law of evidence, who clearly does NOT recommend a total population DNA database for a variety of reasons: Good Day Aly Kindly find the below response 1. Privacy concerns. The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPI Act) was passed in Parliament and is awaiting the proclamation of the President to come into operation. This Act aims to protect personal information of persons and places stringent obligations on the state to ensure the safekeeping, storage and destruction of personal information. A database of DNA will be subjected to the stringent requirements and obligations as set out in the POPI Act. This includes considerations such as the purpose for which the DNA database will kept and what the purpose of the database will be, for what purpose it may it be utilised, the time period for which the personal information may be kept etc. All these requirements will have to be considered to determine the legal implications and feasibility of such a database; 2. During the deliberations of the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Bill in Parliament in 2013, a proposal was made that the DNA of all police officials should be taken. This proposal was rejected in the Portfolio Committee based on considerations of privacy and the financial implications of the proposal. A national database will increase these considerations substantially. 3. Another concern raised in Parliament at that time, was the risk that the police may "plant" the DNA of an innocent person on a crime scene to implicate him in an offence. A national database will increase this risk or the potential that the police will be able to do so. It order to ensure the integrity of the database, proper measures will have to be included to ensure limited access to the database and to protect the safekeeping and storage of the DNA to prevent interference or manipulation thereof. It will pose serious risks to the investigation of offences if DNA may be removed or stolen and there is a perception that the DNA of an innocent person may have been planted at a crime scene; and 4. Legal processes will have to be included to ensure that every person submits a DNA sample. The enforceability of such a requirement will have serious legal implications. Clarification will have to obtained on measures which will be implemented in a person, for example, refuses to submit a sample voluntarily. The legal implication of any enforcement measure will have to comply with constitutional considerations. It is, for example, doubtful that the law will permit a person to be forced to submit a DNA sample against his will. Another consideration in this regard will be the taking and storage of the DNA of undocumented persons and how these matters will be enforced. In view of the above, it is clear that the proposal has serious legal implications. Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 06 December 2019 Script: DNA is a unique identifier that is used as a forensic tool to match a known suspects blood or semen to a sample taken from a crime scene or a rape victim. Vanessa: “The DNA project was an organization I founded in 2004 following the murder of my father.” Vanessa Lynch says police never solved her fathers murder, after he was killed during a home invasion. As police never collected forensic evidence, up until now no one has been convicted. Vanessa: “The reason why I started the DNA project was that I understood that in my father's death that nothing I would do would bring him back personally but I did understand that there were so many people in South Africa that had been affected by crime much the same as our family was affected by crime. And I put a lot of energy and passion into trying to alleviate that situation.” This need to make a chance, resulted in her lobbying government create a criminal DNA database. Vanessa: “Forensic DNA profiling was such a useful forensic tool to resolve murders to solve cold cases. We didn't have the awareness in South Africa to really utilize this incredible technology.” THESE PROFILES WOULD ENABLE LAW ENFORCEMENT TO POTENTIALLY MATCH THEIR DNA TO OTHER CRIMES THEY MAY HAVE COMMITTED, COLD CASES, AS WELL AS OTHER CRIMES THEY MAY COMMIT IN THE FUTURE. University of Pretoria criminologist Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout who has studied violent offenders for 27 years, says they commit many crimes before they’re caught. Bezuidenhout: “On average 100-105 crimes are committed before they're apprehended. Bezuidenhout: “So they’ll start over with the smaller crime, snatch and grab like a mobile phone, and they escalate. We think that many rapists are actually serial rapist, because they get away with it.” That is why convicted offenders were a priority during the discussions resulting in the DNA bill. Vanessa: “The original portfolio committee when passing the bill wanted the convicted offender population to be on the database because they understood that it was a very important part of the forensic DNA database. Recently there was a case for instance of McKee. He was arrested and convicted of an assault for a period of eleven months. His sample was taken at the time that it was able to be taken and that profile was entered onto the convicted offender database. It linked him to 30 unsolved rapes.” The database was a great success - connecting perpetrators to both current and past crimes, but then the testing abruptly ended. Vanessa: “Unfortunately due to issues such as systems not interfacing and training issues they weren't able to put that population on the database within two years.” To fix this, in 2018, the criminal law amendment bill was created allowing correctional services officials to sample the backlog of nearly 47,000 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA - that remain untested. IN THE CURRENT CLIMATE OF A WAR ON WOMEN AND CHILDREN, AND WITH 58 MURDERS AND 114 REPORTED RAPES EVERY DAY, UNLEASHING A VIOLENT DEMOGRAPHIC UPON THE PUBLIC WITHOUT EVEN TAKING THEIR DNA AND FINGERPRINTS SEEMS IRRESPONSIBLE AT BEST, YET THAT IS PRECISELY WHAT IS HAPPENING. AND THE ONE MAN - POLICE MINISTER BHEKI CELE - WHO CAN RECTIFY THIS, HAS DECLINED TO DO SO. Vanessa: “It was simply a technical amendment that was requested of the minister, to say extend this so that we can continue to sample convicted offenders.” THEY WERE INMATES WHO WERE IN JAIL BEFORE THE DNA ACT OF 2013 TOOK EFFECT, AND THEREFORE HAVE BEEN THERE FOR A MINIMUM OF 6 YEARS. Journalist Aly Verbaan has reported on the DNA bill extensively, she says initially Minister Cele agreed the amendment was needed. Verbaan: “On the board's annual report he wrote a about how important it is that he signs this and then within four months, completely turned around.” INSTEAD, CELE HAS DECLINED TO SIGN THE AMENDMENT BILL IN FAVOUR OF MOVING TOWARDS AN UNPRECEDENTED NATIONAL POPULATION DNA DATABASE THAT WOULD REQUIRE EVERY SOUTH AFRICAN CITIZEN TO HAVE A DNA TEST BY WAY OF A BUCCAL SWAB TEST. THIS WOULD THEN BE THE MANDATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HOME AFFAIRS. In February 2019 General Bheki Cele wrote to the Department of Home Affairs after the idea of a population database - containing everyone’s DNA - was proposed during a cabinet committee meeting. Cele’s reasoning for the database was to address the “urgent need to strengthen the country’s crime fighting capacity and conviction of criminals.” Vanessa: “A population database as is a is a fairly controversial idea. It hasn't been enabled anywhere in the world simply because the idea of including all citizens DNA on a database is, it's not something that would would pass constitutional muster.” This is because it would arguably contravene the basic human right to privacy, because our genetic information may be sold or used unethically says Forensic Geneticist Dr Laura Heathfield. Heathfield: “Our legislation has addressed many of the ethical issues surrounding a DNA database for example it stipulates that the DNA sample which contains the full genetic makeup of an individual must be destroyed after a certain period of time.” Vanessa: The difficulty with this approach whilst in theory it probably sounds like a really good idea. Is that you are now undermining the very nature of the retention framework that currently exists in South Africa, because the portfolio committee who were passing the DNA bill originally did not want innocent persons profiles to remain on the database.” Even the police’s own legal department questioned its constitutionality. IN AN EMAIL TO A NUMBER OF HIGH-RANKING SAPS OFFICIALS IN SEPTEMBER THIS YEAR, THEY WERE REMINDED THAT DURING THE DELIBERATION OF THE DNA BILL, THE STATE LAW ADVISOR HAD ADVISED THE PORTFOLIO COMMITTEE ON POLICE, THAT “IT WILL NOT BE CONSTITUTIONAL FOR THE DNA DATABASE TO INCLUDE THE ENTIRE POPULATION.” Verbaan: “It's a non sequitur to say that we are not testing the people who are already guilty of Schedule 8 crimes, and what we're going to do instead is focus on the whole country; we're going to test newborn babies in hospitals, 58 million people, the vast majority of whom have done nothing wrong. How on earth are you going to get people on the street to voluntarily go and give their DNA, their genetic information, to a government?” The department of correctional services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled in 2018. IN ADDITION, MANY SCHEDULE EIGHT OFFENDERS — THOSE CONVICTED OF MURDER, CULPABLE HOMICIDE, RAPE, KIDNAPPING, SEXUAL OFFENCES AGAINST CHILDREN, HUMAN TRAFFICKING, ASSAULT, ROBBERY AND ARSON — WERE RELEASED WITHOUT THEIR DNA PROFILES BEING COLLECTED. Verbaan: “You can collect the DNA at the crime scene but you've got nothing to match it to. We already have them in jail and there’s a law which requires them to give us their DNA. It's just absolutely inexplicable that we can't just get that done.” Studies show that violent criminals are roughly 85-95 percent more likely to reoffend. Bezuidenhout: “If you have a person in prison. 10 years they'll go through all the rehabilitation programs they get out two weeks later they commit the same crime. Jeffrey Thompson, the recent case that killed the elderly couple in Cape Town, he was out on parole and two days later you know commit the crime. Thompson was subsequently sentenced to two life terms, plus 58 years for these murders. The high reoffending rate can be attributed to the lack of prisoner rehabilitation. Bezuidenhout: “We have a very high prison rate, we can accommodate 130,000, we in 165,000. You must have enough professionals; social workers psychologists - the ratio must be very low so that you've got proper professional intervention.” The collection of DNA is a relatively simple process. Heathfield: “We use what's called an easy collect device, and we collect DNA using this foam applicator on the inside of the individual's cheek.” Heathfield calculated the potential cost of just testing the DNA for a national population database. Heathfield: “An Easy collect device costs R163.25. So to just take a sample from a population of 58 million people would cost approximately nine and a half billion rand. And then for DNA profile it would usually cost between 750 and 1000 rand. And it's best practice to do the test in duplicate. So if we're conservative, we would look at an additional 87 billion rand. So altogether over 96 billion rand as a baseline.” FIGURES SHOW THAT 143,260 CONVICTS WERE RELEASED OVER THE PAST TWO YEARS, BUT HOW MANY OF THOSE WERE SCHEDULE EIGHT OFFENDERS OR HOW MANY HAD DNA SAMPLES TAKEN IS UNKNOWN. THE DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONAL SERVICES COULD ALSO NOT PROVIDE ANY FIGURES ON HOW MANY WERE REPEAT OFFENDERS. Aly: “There are people getting out today whose DNA we have not taken who are literally going to kill somebody this week. And that's not that's not my opinion. It's a fact. And this is going to take years even if we got this through the constitution. So here we're going to have schedule eight criminals knowing that they are not on the record.” MINISTER CELE DECLINED AN INTERVIEW WITH CARTE BLANCHE, BECAUSE HE BELIEVES THE DECISION TO HAVE A POPULATION DATABASE LIES WITH THE CONSTITUTIONAL COURT. CELE DID NOT EXPLAIN WHY THE PROPOSED POPULATION DATABASE PRECLUDED THE BACKLOG OF CRIMINALS FROM BEING TESTED IN THE MEANTIME. Aly: “That's the simple question. So the answer keeps coming back. No we were handing it over to Home Affairs.” Like Verbaan we were also referred to the department of home affairs. It says the concept is under consideration and there’s no clear answer yet. The department told Verbaan they had not received Minister Cele’s February letter that proposed the population database. She sent it again, and was surprised by the departmental spokespersons’ quick response. Verbaan: “They dug it, he read the mail on thursday, on the friday,.within a day he'd made up his mind that they're yes they're going to do this, and they seemed to think they’re gonna add DNA database with 58 million people, onto the fingerprints system.” However, Bezuidenhout thinks a population database may be the only way to curb our high crime rate. Bezuidenhout: “My opinion and it might be controversial. I think a database needs to work like fingerprints. Everybody needs to donate DNA. It’s those individuals that raped, a serial, once or two or three, it’s those individuals that got away with stuff that must be worried.” Vanessa: “The immediate solution definitely would be to enable a technical amendment to allow the police to sample parolees prior to them being released from prison. And that if the ministry was very serious about a population database that can happen in parallel to it. When the DNA Act passed I felt it was a victory for a number of South Africans because here was a methodology that could really really identify serial offenders and stop them from continuing to perpetuate crime against vulnerable vulnerable citizens of South Africa. It upsets me terribly that we are not giving it the resources and the dedication that it that it should have in order for us to really do something about crime.

It is about where the money - absolute minimum R5 billion - would come from, AND where is the R20 million that was meant to cover the convict backlog testing? I don’t know the answers re the money. IN the current climate of a veritable war on women and children, and with 58 murders and 114 reported rapes every day, unleashing a violent demographic upon the public without even taking their DNA fingerprint seems irresponsible at best, yet that is precisely what is happening. And the one man - police minister Bheki Cele - who can rectify this has declined to do so.
metadata.Summary: Tens of thousands of dangerous convicts are being released from prison each year but not all of their DNA profiles have been recorded. These profiles would enable law enforcement to potentially match their DNA to other crimes they may have committed, cold cases, as well as any crimes committed by the same offender in future. The Department of Correctional Services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled last year. In addition, many schedule eight offenders — those convicted of murder, culpable homicide, rape, kidnapping, sexual offences against children, human trafficking, assault, robbery and arson — were released without the department collecting their DNA profiles. Cele has failed to sign the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Amendment Bill, drawn up last year, which would allow correctional services officials to take samples of a backlog of 46,727 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA who remain untested. Instead, Cele has declined to sign the amendment bill in favour of moving towards an unprecedented national population DNA database that would require every South African citizen to have a DNA test by way of a buccal (saliva) test. This would then be the mandate of the Department of Home Affairs. Cele's refusal to sign the amendment bill indicates a change of heart since his foreward in the DNA Ethics and Oversight Board's annual report in September last year, in which he wrote that "focus will also be placed on finalising the amendment to the DNA Act which aims to address shortcomings related to the retrospective sampling of offenders serving a sentence for [serious crimes]”. Cele had at that time agreed that the amendment was needed after a two-year "transitional period" expired.
metadata.Further information: "The continuation of the convicted offender sampling programme is essential as the convicted offender index on the National Forensic DNA Database provides an important link to resolving cold cases and apprehending repeat offenders... The conviction and sentencing of serial rapist Sikhangele Mki in September 2017 to 15 life terms demonstrates the importance of ensuring that all convicted offenders are sampled," Cele wrote. The transitional period expired in 2017, leaving more than 46,500 schedule eight convicts unprocessed for DNA. The DCS and the police were not able to process the numbers of prisoners in time because of hold-ups caused by computer interfacing glitches between the departments of police and correctional services, exacerbated by a crippling shortage of sampling kits. Cele's spokesperson Lirandzu Themba said his about-turn was based on advice by the Justice, Crime Prevention & Security. (JCPS) Cluster that “the country embark on a national sampling of all citizens to assist in having a proper DNA database to assist when crime is committed”. However, the constitutionality of Cele's desire for a national DNA database has been called into question by the DA, whose police spokesperson Andrew Whitfield called for the backlog of convicts to be sampled in the short term. "While national government drags its feet on this issue, potential repeat offenders are being released back into society, while SAPS remains with no means of tracking whether these individuals are repeating the offences they were originally convicted of," he said in a statement last month. "The introduction of this bill will add impetus to our fight against gender-based violence. It will ensure that the time needed to convict a repeat offender is minimised, thereby serving justice to victims faster and more efficiently, while freeing up resources for SAPS to pursue more cases and convict more felons.” Whitfield said a national population DNA database was unaffordable, unconstitutional, violated the Bill of Rights, and “wholly unnecessary for the tabling of this Bill”. In an e-mail (which this journalist has in their possession) to a number of high-ranking Saps officials on September 18 this year, Major-General Matilda Manamela of Saps’s Forensic Services Division reminded them that: “The State Law Advisor had advised the Portfolio Committee on Police at the time, during the deliberation of the DNA Bill, that it will not be constitutional for the DNA database to include the population at large.” However, Themba told the Sunday Times that Cele was of the opinion that “only the Constitutional Court can decide on the constitutionality of any matter". Cele declined to explain why the proposed population database precluded the backlog of criminals from being tested in the meantime. Vanessa Lynch, founder of The DNA Project who lobbied support for the for the passing of the DNA Act (in 2013) believes that, at the very least, parolees leaving prison should in the meantime be sampled prior to being released. “If a simple amendment was signed whereby convicted offenders eligible for parole were compelled to submit their sample before being released from prison, this would ensure that serial offenders would be apprehended before committing further crimes, as well as assist with cold cases,” said Lynch. In the current environment where gender-based violence is rife, she believes this to be a reasonable interim solution whilst a White Paper on a population database could be drafted for review without the risk of vulnerable women and children falling prey to serial offenders who could have been identified though DNA before being released. DCS spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo said the only figures the department had were that 143,260 convicts were released over the past two years, but he could not provide figures of how many of those were schedule eight offenders or how many had DNA samples taken. The DCS could also not provide any figures on how many were repeat offenders. Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout of the Department of Social Work and Criminology at the University of Pretoria said while no official government figures for recidivism existed, academic studies put the chances of schedule eight offenders committing further crimes on release or parole at 94%. "South Africa has one of the highest crime rates in the world, as well as some of the highest numbers of incarcerated people, and a very poor rehabilitation programme. In addition, the average criminal in South Africa commits around 100 crimes before being caught. The risk to reward ratio is astoundingly in favour of criminals being tempted back into a life of crime. Prison is the university of crime where, far from being rehabilitated, they learn the tricks of the trade from others and in fact hone their 'skills'. And, most of all, they learn how to justify their criminal behaviour to themselves," said Bezuidenhout. Professor Rudolph Zinn of the Department of Police Practice at Unisa, who has interviewed violent offenders in jail for the past 16 years, said his studies have shown that "criminals generally commit several types of crimes: those caught for robbery also turn out to be rapists and murderers". Bezuidenhout added that, "If a person rapes once, he will do it again". "There is a serial rapist in every rapist. They are virtually unrehabilitatable, especially after having been to prison. They do not learn from their mistakes or from punishment. In addition, violence is so systemic in our jails that they are themselves victimised and traumatised while incarcerated, damaging them further," he said. Cape Town mayoral council member for safety and security, JP Smith, expressed concern about the number of "gangsters" being released from jail in the province. "It used to be about 75 offenders being released every week. Now it is more than 450," he said. Smith cited the recent murder of Russian visitor Ivan Ivanov, who was stabbed to death on Chapman's Peak in July, 10 metres from a parking lot at the start of a hiking trail. One of the three men arrested for the murder had been paroled less than 48 hours earlier for a prior murder conviction. "We are creating our own gang war here," said Smith.

"This would be the competency of Home Affairs and not that of the police department. The police ministry is still waiting for a response on this matter," she said. But it transpired that the correspondence from Cele had not been seen until the DHA was asked for comment. Home Affairs Minister Aaron Motsoaledi said, “The letter from Minister Bheki Cele to the Department of Home Affairs, on February 7 2019 was addressed to the then minister of Home Affairs, Dr Siyabonga Cwele. As Minister of Home Affairs since May 28 2019, I was not aware of this letter, but it was given to me after this query by this journalist. We (minister of Home Affairs, minister of Health, and the Health Ombudsman) did not see the letter addressed to former Home Affairs minister Cwele, but now we are all of common mind with Minister Cele about the development of a population DNA database. We will all work together to make this a possibility. “I must state that I am very much in favour of a population DNA database. Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize has also discussed the possibility of a population DNA database because he is also interested in it. Separately, Health Ombudsman Professor Malegapuru Makgoba also phoned me to ask about the possibility of such a venture. He told me that he is investigating internationally what the practice is. “I met with the Minister of Health and our respective teams on August 5 2019 to discuss a programme whereby new-borns will not be allowed to leave hospitals after birth without an unabridged birth certificate. The possibility of collecting DNA samples at the same time was also discussed. >>> In terms of finance, one buccal swab in the form of an EasiCollect device with an FTA card costs a minimum of R85, says Dr Laura Heathfield, a forensic genetics expert at UCT. Thus, by extrapolation, a minimum of R5 billion will be required to test all 58 million people in the country. This is only the cost of the sample collection device and not laboratory analysis, and also does not take into consideration the substantial infrastructure that would be required for testing, such as centres and laboratories, and the employment of staff to do the tests. MY COMMENTS AND SOME EXPLANATORY NOTES I can also tell you what the international practice is which Makgoba says he is looking into: It has been proposed in many countries, especially first-world ones, but so far the suggestion that every single innocent person be forced to give their genetic information to the state has been declared unconstitutional and an infringement on the right to privacy… eg. Portugal, UAE, France, Canada. 1. No country has yet managed an entire pop database, only very extensive forensic ones. It would be miraculous if SA was the first country in the world to get a national population database! And some very first-world countries only have 5 million people and they have not managed it, in theory, in law, or in practice. “In the expansive group [of countries that have a forensic database], the inclusion criteria in most countries allow that individuals suspected of any crime can be submitted to sample collection and, consequently, to the inclusion of their respective DNA profiles in the forensic database.” and “[Internationally] the ethical challenges of forensic DNA databases have usually been approached as potential threats to a range of civil rights, such as the right to privacy, liberty and moral and physical integrity, the dignity of persons, and the presumption of innocence.” https://jme.bmj.com/content/41/10/820.info https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6533668/ 2. We have already seen in SA that police officers could not be tested (to exclude their DNA from crime scenes) as it was seen to be an infringement of their rights. 3. Even in forensic (ie criminal databases) there are strict codes that apply to discarding genetic info if a person is found innocent, or after a certain period of time after they have been released, etc. So criminals’ rights to genetic privacy are considered worldwide — how then would innocent citizens feel about being forced to provide their genetic data? 4. [Getting into what can be done with people’s private genetic info is obviously way beyond the scope of this article, but if not strictly regulated, it can be sold to medical companies, planted at crime scenes, as well as used to discriminate on grounds of race or gender, among other concerns.] Here is a mail from Brigadier Marga van Rooyen, SAPS Division of Legal and Policy Services, an expert academic and author in law of evidence, who clearly does NOT recommend a total population DNA database for a variety of reasons: Good Day Aly Kindly find the below response 1. Privacy concerns. The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPI Act) was passed in Parliament and is awaiting the proclamation of the President to come into operation. This Act aims to protect personal information of persons and places stringent obligations on the state to ensure the safekeeping, storage and destruction of personal information. A database of DNA will be subjected to the stringent requirements and obligations as set out in the POPI Act. This includes considerations such as the purpose for which the DNA database will kept and what the purpose of the database will be, for what purpose it may it be utilised, the time period for which the personal information may be kept etc. All these requirements will have to be considered to determine the legal implications and feasibility of such a database; 2. During the deliberations of the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Bill in Parliament in 2013, a proposal was made that the DNA of all police officials should be taken. This proposal was rejected in the Portfolio Committee based on considerations of privacy and the financial implications of the proposal. A national database will increase these considerations substantially. 3. Another concern raised in Parliament at that time, was the risk that the police may "plant" the DNA of an innocent person on a crime scene to implicate him in an offence. A national database will increase this risk or the potential that the police will be able to do so. It order to ensure the integrity of the database, proper measures will have to be included to ensure limited access to the database and to protect the safekeeping and storage of the DNA to prevent interference or manipulation thereof. It will pose serious risks to the investigation of offences if DNA may be removed or stolen and there is a perception that the DNA of an innocent person may have been planted at a crime scene; and 4. Legal processes will have to be included to ensure that every person submits a DNA sample. The enforceability of such a requirement will have serious legal implications. Clarification will have to obtained on measures which will be implemented in a person, for example, refuses to submit a sample voluntarily. The legal implication of any enforcement measure will have to comply with constitutional considerations. It is, for example, doubtful that the law will permit a person to be forced to submit a DNA sample against his will. Another consideration in this regard will be the taking and storage of the DNA of undocumented persons and how these matters will be enforced. In view of the above, it is clear that the proposal has serious legal implications.
